name: Rıfkı
description: Rıfkı (also known as Turkish King) is a compendium trick-taking game for four players, widely played in Turkey. It is the Turkish variation of King (Barbu). Twenty hands are played; each player declares five contracts (two trump, three negative). Rıfkı refers to the King of Heartsâ€”which scores -320 to the player who wins it in that contract.

history.origins: Derived from the French game Barbu (The Bearded Man, referring to the King of Hearts). It was adapted in Turkey with specific scoring weights that emphasize the penalty of the King of Hearts (Rıfkı).
timeline: 1950s: The name Rıfkı becomes synonymous with the King of Hearts in Turkish slang.
1980s: Becomes a social staple for university students and tea-house culture.
Present: One of the top-rated social strategy games in Turkey, often played digitally.
history.cultural: In Turkey, taking Rıfkı (the King of Hearts) is often met with lighthearted ridicule and high-intensity social commentary.
history.evolution: The scoring system transformed into a zero-sum (or near zero-sum) balance where the massive negatives are offset by high-value positive 'Trump' rounds.

setup.dealing: Dealer shuffles; player opposite cuts. Deal all 52 cards counter-clockwise (13 each). First declarer is the holder of the Two of Diamonds; positions rotate counter-clockwise for 20 hands.

rules.objective: Over 20 hands, each player declares five contracts (two trump, three negative). In trump contracts each trick won scores +50; in negative contracts certain cards or tricks incur penalties. The player with the highest net score after all 20 hands wins.
rules.gameplay: Must follow suit. In trump contracts, must trump if unable to follow (even underruff). In negative contracts, no trumps; if unable to follow, discard a penalty card if you have one. In Rıfkı and Kupa (Hearts), hearts may not be led unless already broken or you have only hearts. Penalty cards must be played when a higher card of the suit has been played to the trick.
keyRules: Each player declares five contracts over 20 hands (two trump, three negative). Each negative contract type can be declared only twice per game. Declarer leads to the first trick. Winner of each trick leads to the next. In trump contracts each trick scores +50; in negative contracts penalty cards or specified tricks score negative points.

strategy.basic: Assess Your Hand. If you have many high cards (Aces/Kings), use them in your Positive (Trump) rounds to rack up +50s. If you have low cards or a 'Void' in a suit, choose 'Rıfkı' or 'Girls'. The most important rule is: DON'T LEAD Rıfkı (King of Hearts) unless you have toâ€”once it is out, the tension of that round vanishes.
strategy.intermediate: Contract Exhaustion: Keep track of which negative contracts haven't been played yet. If 'Last Two' is still available and you have low cards, wait for someone else to lead a high-card round. Also, if you know an opponent is desperate to play a positive round, 'Trump' their high cards as early as possible to minimize their gain.
strategy.advanced: The 'Rıfkı' Trap: In the Rıfkı round, if you hold the Queen or Jack of Hearts, you are in a power position. You can 'Flush Out' the King of Hearts from whoever holds it by leading small hearts. If *you* hold the King of Hearts, try to play it on an opponent's Ace lead as quickly as possible to get rid of the -320 penalty early.
tips: In 'No Tricks' (El Almaz), lean on your 2s and 3s. If you are forced to lead a King, you are almost guaranteed to take the penalty.
Never choose a Trump contract if your hand is balancedâ€”you need a 'Long' suit (5+ cards) to make trumps effective.

scoring.description: Trump contract: +50 per trick to winner (total +650). Negative contracts: Rıfkı (K♥) -320; Kız (Queens) -100 each; Erkek (Kings and Jacks) -60 each; Kupa (Hearts) -30 each; Son İki (last two tricks) -180 each; El Almaz (each trick) -50. Highest net after 20 rounds wins.

synthesis.shortDescription: Rıfkı (Turkish King) is a four-player compendium trick-taking game: 20 hands, two trump and three negative contracts per player. Highest net score wins.
